extracted.intended_audience: editors, copyeditors, typesetters, authors, and publishers applying a house punctuation style
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guidance for punctuation and hyphenation as defined by a house style (University of Chicago Press). Covers when and how to use periods, commas, colons, semicolons, dashes, parentheses, brackets, ellipses, apostrophes, quotation marks, and hyphens, plus special cases and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: General punctuation style (rule 121)
rubrics_metrics.description: All punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: print punctuation in same type as preceding word/letter. (Examples in original: "With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill"; Luke 4:16a; No. i.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Period: end of sentence (rule 122)
rubrics_metrics.description: A period is used to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See additional rules (125) for exceptions (running-heads, headlines, signatures, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations and symbol exceptions (rule 123)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except in cases where a mechanical necessity compels the omission of a letter or letters in the middle of a word for which there is no recognized abbreviated form; such omission is indicated by an apostrophe. Treat the metric symbols as abbreviations, but not the chemical symbols, nor the phrase 'per cent,' nor the format of books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. i, Chas., ibid., S.V.; 10 mm.; but: m'f'g pl't (= manufacturing plant); O, Fe; 2 per cent; 4to, 8vo. Exceptions: do not use a period after recognized abbreviations for linguistic epochs or after initials of well-known publications (IE, OE, MHG, AJSL, ZAW, CIL) nor after MS (= manuscript). Notes mention journal-specific exceptions for spacing/period use with measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No period after Roman numerals (rule 124)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use no period after Roman numerals, even if having the value of ordinals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. IV; Louis XVI was on the throne.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit period after certain heads and lines (rule 125)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omit the period after running-heads; after centered headlines; after side-heads set in separate lines; after cut-in heads; after box-heads in tables; and after superscriptions and legends which do not form a complete sentence; after date lines at top of communications, and after signatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-reference to rule 50 for explanation of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period placement with quotation marks and parentheses (rule 126)
rubrics_metrics.description: The period is placed inside the quotation marks; and inside the parentheses when the matter inclosed is an independent sentence and forms no part of the preceding sentence; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tennyson's "In Memoriam." Put the period inside the quotation marks. (This is a rule without exception.) When the parentheses form part of the preceding sentence, put the period outside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclamation point usage and placement (rules 127-128)
rubrics_metrics.description: The exclamation point is used to mark an outcry, or an emphatic or ironical utterance. The exclamation point is placed inside the quotation marks when part of the quotation; otherwise outside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Long live the king!" "Heaven forbid!" Placement illustrated with quoted material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrogation point (question mark) usage and placement (rules 129-130)
rubrics_metrics.description: The interrogation point is used to mark a query, or to express a doubt. Indirect questions should not be followed by an interrogation point. The interrogation point should be placed inside the quotation marks only when it is a part of the quotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Who is this?"; indirect question: He asked whether he was ill. Quotation example: The question: "Who is who, and what is what?"

rubrics_metrics.name: Colon usage (rules 131-136)
rubrics_metrics.description: The colon marks a discontinuity of grammatical construction greater than that indicated by the semicolon and less than that indicated by the period. Common uses: (i) emphasize a close connection between two clauses which might be separated by a period; (ii) separate a clause which is grammatically complete from a second which contains an illustration or amplification; (iii) introduce a formal statement, extract, or speech in dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comma before quotation of a clause in the middle of a sentence. Use a colon after salutatory phrases in letters, between chapter and verse in Scripture passages and between hours and minutes, and between place of publication and publisher in literary references. Place colon outside quotation marks unless part of quotation. Numerous examples illustrate each usage and counterexamples (when to use comma instead).

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicolon usage (rules 137-140)
rubrics_metrics.description: A semicolon is used to mark the division of a sentence somewhat more independent than that marked by a comma. Use a semicolon in enumerations between lengthy or complex items, especially when items contain internal punctuation. In Scripture references, use semicolon to separate passages containing chapters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Semicolon should be placed outside the quotation marks unless part of the quotation. Examples include linking clauses where 'for' is commonly preceded by a semicolon, and complex enumerations with internal punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma rules and principal uses (rules 141-162)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comma is used to indicate the smallest interruptions in continuity of thought or grammatical construction, marking separations that contribute to clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive subrules and examples included: separate proper nouns for different individuals/places (142); use comma before final 'and/or' in a series (143) with exceptions for close-knit phrases; normally put commas before/after clauses introduced by conjunctions when a change of subject occurs (144) with exceptions; introductory adverbial/connective words (now, then, however, therefore, moreover, etc.) should be followed or set off by commas when they introduce inference or explanation (145) with exceptions; omit comma before 'rather' in some expressions (146); limit comma between adjectives when last adjective directly relates to noun (147); set off participial clauses usually with commas (148); comma before 'not' introducing an antithetical clause (149); use commas for parenthetical/adverbial/appositional clauses and dashes for both structural and logical disconnection, never both together (150); use comma to separate identical/closely similar words for clarity (151); commas to set off complementary/qualifying adjectives (152); commas to separate co-ordinate clauses that end in a word governing another clause (153); use comma to separate two numbers (154); comma for ellipsis/omission of repeated words (155); comma before brief direct quotations (156); comma before 'of' with residence/position (157) with exceptions; do not use comma between consecutive pages in references (158) except scriptural references; comma after digits indicating thousands (159) with journal exceptions; separate month and year with comma (160) with exceptions; omit comma in signatures and at beginning of articles after author name followed by address/position lines (161); comma always placed inside quotation marks (162). Examples provided for each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe usage (rules 163-165)
rubrics_metrics.description: An apostrophe marks the omission of letters in contractions and figures in numbers; forms the possessive case of common and proper nouns by adding an apostrophe or apostrophe + s; forms the plural of numerals and of rare/artificial noun-coinages by adding an apostrophe + s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ne'er, don't, 'twas; class of '96. Possessive examples: a man's, horses' tails, Scott's Ivanhoe, Jones's farms, Themistocles' era. Plural-of-numeral examples: in the 1900's; the Y.M.C.A.'s. Rules for proper names ending in sibilants described (monosyllabic vs multisyllabic treatments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks (reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks rules are given in the section on 'Quotations' (see rules 74-91).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page references the dedicated quotation section (74-91) but does not reproduce that content here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dashes: use and restrictions (rules 166-175)
rubrics_metrics.description: A dash denotes a sudden break, stop, transition, long pause, or an abrupt/epigrammatic turn of sentiment. Use dashes for parenthetical clauses that are both logically and structurally independent; for emphasis or expansion where a repeated word/phrase is explained; where 'namely' is implied; to precede a final summarizing clause; and in certain headline and list contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dash for side-heads and in place of 'to' connecting words or numbers (en-dash vs em-dash distinctions illustrated). Let a dash precede references following a direct quotation of at least one complete sentence in footnotes. Do not ordinarily use a dash in connection with any other point except a period; avoid combining dashes and commas in certain constructions. Examples and counterexamples are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses usage and enumeration notation (rules 176-177)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place figures or letters between parentheses to mark divisions in enumerations run into the text. If divisions are paragraphed, use single parentheses for lower-case italic letters and a period with figures and capital letters. Parentheses should not ordinarily be used for parenthetical clauses unless confusion might arise or the clause is wholly irrelevant to the main argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives an ordinary notation/indention scheme for multi-level enumerations (A., I., 1., a), (i), (a), etc.) and examples of when parentheses are preferable to dashes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brackets usage (rule 178-179)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used to inclose an explanation or note, to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, to rectify a mistake, to supply an omission, and for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: editorial notes inside brackets, bracketed interpolations in quotations, citation corrections (e.g., [second edition]). Also instructs that phrases such as '[Continued from p. ___]' or '[To be concluded]' should be placed between brackets, centered, and set in italics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses usage and formatting (rules 180-181)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate the omission of one or more words not essential to the idea. For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence four periods, separated by a space (en-quad), should ordinarily be used, except in very narrow measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If whole paragraphs or lines are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length; do not extend periods beyond the length of the longest type-line. If preceding line ends in a point, that point should not be included in the four. An ellipsis is part of the citation and should be enclosed in quotation marks. Examples demonstrate usage in prose and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation and compounds (rules 182-196)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on use of hyphens: hyphenate at line breaks between syllables; hyphenate compound adjectives preceding a noun; hyphenate many compound nouns formed by two nouns in objective relation; hyphenate present participle + noun compounds and certain absolute forms; and detailed rules for when to hyphenate combinations with book/house/mill/room/shop/work depending on syllable count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive subrules and exceptions: do not hyphenate with adverbs ending in '-ly' or when adjective phrase follows the noun; rules and examples for nouns formed by two-noun combinations (mind-reader vs lawgiver exception); scheme for compounds formed with one-, two-, or three-syllable prefixes (handbook vs pocket-book vs reference book); rules for 'maker'/'dealer' compounds, 'store' compounds depending on syllable count, 'fellow-' always hyphenated, family-relation compounds hyphenated, 'great-' for degree hyphenated, 'life'/'world' compounds hyphenated (with lifetime exception), 'skin' compounds rules, 'master-' and 'god-' compounds, and that 'half', 'quarter', etc. combined with a noun should be followed by a hyphen. Numerous examples accompany each rule.
